Enhancing energy recovery from corn straw via two-stage anaerobic
digestion with stepwise microaerobic hydrogen fermentation and
methanogenesis

Keywords:
Two-stage anaerobic digestion
Microaeration
Hydrogen fermentation
Methanogenesis
Corn straw
Energy recovery
a b s t r a c t
Anaerobic digestion (AD) technology attracts increasing concerns for organic waste disposal, renewable
energy production as well as organic fertilizer preparation. However, the AD of cellulosic substrate is
limited by low efﬁciency. Microaeration has recently been used to improve the AD efﬁciency. However,
the inhibition of methanogenesis by microaeration limited its application. To enhance the energy re-
covery from AD of corn straw and avoid the inhibition of microaeration on methanogenesis, two-stage
AD including microaerobic hydrogen fermentation (stage I) and methanogenesis (stage II) was investi-
gated. Results showed microaeration had beneﬁcial effects on hydrogen fermentation, methane pro-
duction and energy recovery depending on the oxygen loading level. At the optimized initial pH of 7.5 for
hydrogen production, microaerobic hydrogen fermentation achieved the maximum hydrogen yield of
24.3 mL/g VS (volatile solid, 37 C and normal pressure) with the oxygen loading of 5 mL/g VS, which was
70% higher than that without microaeration. Overall, the two-stage AD performed better in methane
yield and energy recovery than one-stage AD. When the oxygen loading during hydrogen fermentation
was 10 mL/g VS of corn straw, the maximum total energy recovery of 10.6 kJ/g VS was obtained, which
was 18% higher than that of one-stage AD. The two-stage AD consisting of microaerobic hydrogen
fermentation (stage I) and methanogenesis (stage II) is a promising way to enhance the energy recovery
from AD of cellulosic substrates like corn straw.

1. Introduction
Anaerobic digestion (AD) technology has been widely applied in
the disposal of organic waste (Ye et al., 2018). Given its efﬁcient
performance in waste reduction and energy recovery, AD receives
increasing interests in the research community and the public
worldwide (Nielfa et al., 2015). The high methane content (around
50e70%) in biogas makes it suitable for replacing traditional energy
sources (Esen and Yuksel, 2013; Baena-Moreno et al., 2019).
Agricultural wastes, such as corn and wheat straw are abundant
and rich in carbohydrate contents, which have been demonstrated
as potential sources for bioenergy production via AD technology
(He et al., 2018; Mahmoodi et al., 2018). However, the compact
structure and complex composition of cellulosic agriculture wastes
lead to low AD efﬁciency, which is one of the challenges for the AD
of agricultural wastes. Measures including substrate pretreatment
(Wang et al., 2017), co-digestion (Jin et al., 2018; Thanarasu et al.,
2018), bioaugmentation (Zhang et al., 2015) and combination of
these technologies (Mulat et al., 2018) have been extensively taken
to improve the AD performance. However, some inherent short-
comings such as extra energy input, chemicals requirement, and/or
the suitability limitation for scale-up exist in these measures (Lim
and
Wang,

compounds; co-digestion is not efﬁcient enough in the improve-
ment of methane yield, which is also limited by the substrate
supply; the long-term and steady subculture of selected microor-
ganism is a problem for bioaugmentation technology (Wei, 2016).
Therefore, explorations for simple and practical methods to
improve the efﬁciency are urgently needed to further advance the
applications of AD technology.
Recently, microaeration, which means introducing of limited
oxygen/air into the anaerobic digester (ranged from 0.005 to 5 L O2/
L reactor/day according to different studies) (Nguyen and Khanal,
2018), has been found to be an efﬁcient method to improve the
AD performance of organic wastes (Fu et al., 2016b; Tsapekos et al.,
2017). As reported, microaeration could regulate the microbial
community structure by stimulating the growth of certain facul-
tative microorganism, thus leading to higher hydrolysis efﬁciency
(Fu et al., 2016b; Lim et al., 2014). Microorganisms afﬁliating to
phylum Firmicutes were reported to play a key role in microaeration
(Fu et al., 2016a; Lim et al., 2014). However, the methanogenesis of
AD, which is carried out by methanogens, is sensitive to oxygen.
Though some researchers reported methanogenic microorganisms
such as Methanobacterium and Methanosarcina can tolerate to
limited oxygen (dissolved oxygen up to 5.6 mg/L) (Nguyen and
Khanal, 2018; Botheju and Bakke, 2011), microaeration during AD
could inhibit the methanogenesis process at certain level of oxygen
loading. It is challenging to balance the positive effect and negative
effect of microaeration during AD. As such, two-stage AD, in which
the AD process is separated into the hydrolysis/acidogensis (stage I)
and methanogenesis (stage II) that are optimized individually
(Algapani et al., 2018; Tijani et al., 2018) could be a potential so-
lution for the problem of the application of microaeration in AD.
According to a two-stage AD including microaerobic hydrogen
fermentation and methanogenesis, the inhibition of oxygen on
methanogenesis could be avoid by preventing the contiguity of
oxygen
and
methanogens.
Improved
hydrogen
yield
under
microaeration condition has also been reported in previous study
(Li et al., 2016). Actually, the hydrogen fermentation stage of two-
stage AD could also be considered as biological pretreatment
method for organic solid waste, during the hydrogen fermentation
hydrogen energy recovery as well as substrate pretreatment could
be achieved simultaneously (Ariunbaatar et al., 2014). Microaera-
tion during hydrogen fermentation stage could obtain a higher
hydrolysis of complex substrates due to the higher production of
hydrolytic enzymes, thus beneﬁt the following methane fermen-
tation (Lim and Wang, 2013). Through two-stage AD might operate
a little difﬁcultly, two-stage AD of cellulosic substrate was reported
to be more stable and efﬁcient than one-stage AD, which recovered
more energy from substrates (Nathao et al., 2013).
In order to improve the stability and energy recovery of the AD
process while avoiding the inhibition of oxygen on methano-
genesis, two-stage AD of corn straw including microaerobic
hydrogen fermentation (stage I) and methanogenesis (stage II) was
examined in this study. The initial pH and the oxygen loading for
microaerobic hydrogen production were optimized. The traditional
two-stage and one-stage AD without microaeration were also
performed as controls to reﬂect the effects of microaeration and
two-stage approaches on the AD process. In addition, energy re-
covery from AD of corn straw was also calculated based on the
hydrogen and methane yields. The implementation of this study
could offer an efﬁcient and simple way to enhance the energy re-
covery from cellulosic substrates like corn straw through AD
technology.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Substrate and inoculum
Air-dried corn straw (dried in the ﬁeld) was collected from the
ﬁeld of Lianyungang (Jiangsu province, China) as substrate. Before
used, the corn straw was chopped and sieved to size of less than
0.5 cm by 0.5 cm sieve. Anaerobic sludge collected from an anaer-
obic digester of Tuandao Water Treatment Plant that mainly treats
urban sewage (Qingdao, Shandong province, China, mainly treats
urban sewage) was used as inoculum. The collected inoculum was
concentrated using centrifuge method and stored in a refrigerator
at 4 C. Before fermentation experiment, the inoculum was acti-
vated in a shaking water bath at 37 C with the shaking speed of
120 rpm for 3 days. The characteristics of the substrate and inoc-
ulum are shown in Table 1.
2.2. Experimental designs
2.2.1. Optimization of initial pH for hydrogen production
Optimization of initial pH for hydrogen production was con-
ducted in 300 mL glass bottles with a working volume of 150 mL.
Prior to the start of the hydrogen fermentation of two-stage AD, the
inoculum was ﬁrstly heated at 80 C for 15 min to suppress the
activity of methanogens and enrich the hydrogen-producing mi-
croorganisms (Raﬁeenia et al., 2017). During the optimization of
initial pH for hydrogen production, 5.33 g (TS) corn straw and 1.33 g
(TS) heat-treated anaerobic sludge were mixed in the sterile bot-
tles, and the working volumes were adjusted to 150 mL by adding
distilled water. The designed initial pH for optimization included
4.5, 5.5, 6.5, 7.5, and 8.5. The pHs of the fermentation systems were
adjusted to designed initial pH with NaOH (2 M) and HCl (2 M)
solutions, and the pH values were no longer adjusted during the
hydrogen fermentation process. All the bottles were ﬂushed with
N2 for 5 min to remove the oxygen and sealed with rubber stoppers.
Then, all the bottles were incubated in a shaking water bath at 37 C
with the shaking speed of 120 rpm until the daily biogas yield was
less than 1% of the cumulative biogas yield.

2.2.2. Microaeration during the hydrogen fermentation of two-
stage AD
With the predetermined optimal initial pH in section 2.2.1, the
effects of microaeration on the hydrogen fermentation of the two-
stage AD were studied. The procedure of this process was in
accordance with Section 2.2.1. The designated total amount of ox-
ygen during the whole microaerobic hydrogen fermentation pro-
cess were 0, 5, 10, 20, and 40 mL/g VS (total VS of corn straw and
inoculum, marked as Two-stage 0, Two-stage 5, Two-stage 10, Two-
stage 20, and Two-stage 40, respectively). The Two-stage 0 meant
two-stage AD without microaeration, which was conducted as a
control to reﬂect the effect of microaeration. The needed oxygen
was calculated based on the designed oxygen load and the mass of
corn straw added, then injected into the sealed reactors daily using
syringe. The fermentation time was 5 days according to the results
of section 2.2.1.
2.2.3. Methane fermentation of one- and two-stage AD
After the hydrogen fermentation stage, the bottles were opened
and re-inoculated with 1.33 g fresh anaerobic sludge (TS) to initiate
the methane fermentation stage. The working volumes were
adjusted to 200 mL by adding distilled water and the pHs were
adjusted to 7.5 with NaOH (2 M) and HCl (2 M). Then, all the bottles
were ﬂushed with N2 for 5 min to remove the oxygen and sealed
with rubber stoppers. The one-stage AD of corn straw was also run
in parallel, where 5.33 g corn straw (TS) and 2.66 g anaerobic sludge
(TS) were charged into the bottles to which a certain amount of
distilled water was added to increase the working volume to
200 mL. The pH adjustment and bottle purging were done by
following the same procedures used for the two-stage AD. Finally,
all the bottles were incubated at 37 C with 120 rpm in a shaking
water bath for methane fermentation until the daily biogas yield
was less than 1% of the cumulative biogas yield. Each treatment was
run in triplicate unless speciﬁed, otherwise.

2.4. Analytical methods
The methane and hydrogen concentrations in biogas were
measured with a gas chromatograph (GC, SP6890, Shandong Lunan
Inc., China) equipped with a thermal conductivity detector (TCD)
and Porapak Q chromatographic column (180 cm  Ø3mm). The
carrier gases for methane and hydrogen tests were argon and ni-
trogen, respectively. The temperatures of the injector, detector, and
oven were 100, 100 and 80 C, respectively. The TS and VS were
measured according to a standard method (APHA, 2006). The cel-
lulose, hemicellulose and lignin contents of corn straw were
measured by using the method of Goering and van Soest (1970).
Element and pH were measured with elemental analyzer (Vario EL
III elemental analyzer) and pH meter (B-212, HORIBA), respectively.
To measure volatile fatty acids (VFAs), the liquid samples were
ﬁrstly centrifuged at 10,000 rpm for 5 min, and the supernatants
were ﬁltered through a 0.45 mm glass microﬁber ﬁlter and acidized
to pH of 2.5 using 2 M HCl before GC analysis. VFAs were analyzed
on a GC (GC-2014, SHIMADZU) equipped with Innowax column
(30m*0.25 mm*0.25m) and a ﬂame ion-ization detectors (FID). The
temperatures of the injector and detector were 220 C, respectively.
The temperature of the oven was set to increase from 25 C to
180 C at the speed of 10 C/min.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Anaerobic hydrogen yield at different initial pH
The pH value has a great inﬂuence on the growth of acidogenic
microorganisms and play a crucial role in the acidogenesis step of
two-stage AD system (Ravi et al., 2018). In this study, the initial pH
was optimized at the initial pH values of 4.5, 5.5, 6.5, 7.5, and 8.5
toward the highest hydrogen yield. The hydrogen fermentation was
S.-F. Fu et al. / Journal of Cleaner Production 247 (2020) 119651
3

conducted until the daily biogas yield was less than 1% of the cu-
mulative biogas yield. Actually, after 5th day of fermentation, all of
the hydrogen yields decreased rapidly (there were no biogas yield
at the initial pH of 4.5, 5.5 and 6.5). Therefore, the running time for
hydrogen fermentation in this study was set as 5 days. The tem-
poral cumulative hydrogen yield with different initial pH values are
shown in Fig. 1. The initial pH showed signiﬁcant effect on the
hydrogen yield of corn straw. The 5-day cumulative hydrogen yields
at the initial pH values of 4.5, 5.5, 6.5, 7.5, and 8.5 were 6, 5.9, 9.4,
13.7, and 6.5 mL/g VS (37 C and normal pressure) corn straw,
respectively. Statistical analysis by T-test: a pairwise comparisons
was conducted with the software of Microsoft Ofﬁce Excel 2016).
Results showed the hydrogen yields at the initial pH values of 4.5,
5.5, and 8.5 had no signiﬁcant difference with each other (p > 0.05).
The hydrogen yields at the initial pH of 6.5 and 7.5 were statistical
higher than others. When the initial pH increased from 7.5 to 8.5,
the hydrogen yield decreased signiﬁcantly (p < 0.5). The lower
Hydrogenase activity at higher pH value could be the reason for this
phenomenon (Kim et al., 2011).
The results obtained in this study are similar to the previous
study conducted by Kim et al. (2011), who reported the optimized
initial pH for hydrogen fermentation of food waste was 8.0. How-
ever, due to the complex structure corn straw, the maximum
hydrogen yield from corn straw at the initial pH of 7.5 was lower
than that from food waste (Nathao et al., 2013) or waste activated
sludge (Wan et al., 2016). In this research, pH 7.5 was selected for all
the following studies.
3.2. Effect of microaeration on hydrogen fermentation of two-stage
AD
3.2.1. Hydrogen production
Microaerobic hydrogen fermentations were conducted at the
initial pH value of 7.5 that optimized from the Section 3.1.
Microaerobic condition is deﬁned by Nguyen and Khanal (2018)
as introduction of small amount of air or oxygen (typically
ranged from 0.005 to 5 L O2/L reactor/day) into an anaerobic
system. In this study, microaerobic hydrogen fermentation lasted
for 5 days, during which the microaerobic condition was created
by daily oxygen injection with a syringe into the headspace of the
bottles. The cumulative hydrogen yields at different oxygen load
were shown in Fig. 2. Statistical analysis of the effects of oxygen
loads on hydrogen yields were also analyzed by T-test: a pairwise
comparisons. Results showed the oxygen injected into the system
affected the hydrogen yield signiﬁcantly (p < 0.05). The cumu-
lative hydrogen yields ranked in the order of Two-stage 5 > Two-
stage 10 > Two-stage 0 > Two-stage 20 > Two-stage 40.
Maximum hydrogen yield of 22.7 mL/g VS (37 C and normal
pressure) was obtained with the oxygen loading of 5 mL/g VS,
which is 67% higher than that of Two-stage 0 (anaerobic
hydrogen
fermentation
without
microaeration).
Improved
hydrogen yield under microaerobic condition was also reported
by Li et al. (2016) who indicated that the microaerobic condition
could beneﬁt the hydrolysis of the substrate, leading to higher
hydrogen yield. Improved hydrolysis process under microaerobic
condition was widely reported (Montalvo et al., 2016). The
microaerobic condition could stimulate the growth of anaerobic/
facultative microorganisms to produce more extracellular en-
zymes, leading to higher hydrolysis efﬁciency (Girotto et al.,
2016; Lim et al., 2014). However, excessive oxygen loadings
over 5 mL/g VS had insigniﬁcant positive (i.e., 10 mL/g VS on day
5, compared to Two-stage 0) and even inhibitory effect (e.g., 20
and 40 mL/g VS) on hydrogen yield. As shown in Fig. 2, the
hydrogen yield at the oxygen loading of 10 mL/g VS had no
obvious difference with that of Two-stage 0 (p > 0.05). Further-
more, hydrogen yields at the oxygen loadings of 20 and 40 mL/g
VS were signiﬁcantly lower than that of Two-stage 0 (p < 0.05).
Especially at the oxygen loading of 40 mL/g VS, the hydrogen
yield was extremely inhibited and was only 2.8 mL/g VS (37 C
and normal pressure), which means the activities of hydro-
genogens
were
signiﬁcantly
inhibited.
Hydrogenogens
are
responsible for the conversion of simple sugars to hydrogen and
organic acid during the hydrogen fermentation stage of AD
process (Lin et al., 2018), but most of them are sensitive to oxy-
gen.
Therefore,
the
hydrogen production process
could
be
inhibited in the presence of overdosed oxygen (e.g., oxygen

loading over 10 mL/g VS in this research).
3.2.2. VFA production
VFAs are the by-products of the hydrogen fermentation pro-
cess. In current study, the VFA concentrations were measured
daily using a GC (Gas Chromatography). The daily VFA concen-
trations are showed in Fig. 3. The VFA concentrations increased
with the time. After 2 days of hydrogen fermentation, the VFA
concentrations in AD reactors with oxygen addition were always
higher than that in AD reactor without oxygen. The 5-day VFA
concentrations with different levels of oxygen loading ranked in
the order of Two-stage 5 > Two-stage 10 > Two-stage 20 > Two-
stage 40 > Two-stage 0. The higher VFA concentrations in the
presence of limited oxygen might be attributed to the higher
hydrolysis efﬁciency under microaerobic condition (Li et al.,
2016; Lim and Wang, 2013). However, excessive oxygen might
result in decreased VFA concentration (e.g., Two-stage 20 and
Two-stage 40), which could be explained by the further oxi-
dization of VFAs under higher oxygen loadings (Nguyen et al.,
2019).
During the whole hydrogen fermentation process, acetate and
butyrate were the main VFAs, which took up more than 70% of the
total VFAs. In addition, the proportion of acetate and butyrate in
VFAs increased with the time. As reported, acetate and butyrate
fermentation are the main metabolic pathways involved in
hydrogen production (shown as Eqs. (4) and (5)) (Łukajtis et al.,
2018). The main metabolic pathways of hydrogen production in
the current study were still acetate and butyrate fermentation,
which indicated that the microaerobic conditions did not alter the
hydrogen production pathway.

3.3. Methane production during the methane fermentation stage of
the two-stage AD
3.3.1. Daily and cumulative methane yields
Due to the accumulation of VFAs during the hydrogen fermen-
tation (Fig. 3), the pHs of the reactors dropped from 7.5 to 6.1e6.3.
After re-inoculation of the fresh AD sludge for the methane
fermentation in the 2nd stage, the pHs of the reactors were
adjusted to 7.5 with NaOH (2 M) and HCl (2 M). Daily and cumu-
lative methane yields during the methane fermentation are shown
in Fig. 4. All the daily methane yields of two-stage AD and one-stage
AD showed two peaks, and the daily methane yields after micro-
aerobic hydrogen fermentation were generally higher than those of
one-stage and Two-stage 0 at the initial 10 days of methane
fermentation (Fig. 4a). These could beneﬁt from the high VFA
concentrations that were produced during the hydrogen fermen-
tation (Fig. 3).
Methane fermentation stage lasted for 45 days. The cumulative
methane yields of different AD scenarios showed signiﬁcant dif-
ference (p < 0.05, Fig. 4b). The overall cumulative methane yields of
two-stage AD were higher than that of one-stage. The respective
cumulative methane yields of Two-stage 0, Two-stage 5, Two-stage
10, Two-stage 20 and Two-stage 40 were 264.5, 287.8, 296.0, 285.5,
and 270.6 mL/g VS (37 C and normal pressure), which were 3.6%,
12.7%, 15.9%, 11.8%, and 6.0% higher than that of one-stage,
respectively. This result is consistent with previous reports (Akobi
et al., 2016; Gioannis et al., 2017). When comparing the energy
recovery from one- and two-stage anaerobic digestion of food
waste, Gioannis et al. (2017) reported 19% higher methane yield
was obtained from two-stage AD than that of one-stage AD. Simi-
larly, Akobi et al. (2016) also found the two-stage AD of extruded
lignocellulosic biomass obtained 11% higher methane yield than
the one-stage.
Microaeration during the hydrogen fermentation stage gener-
ated positive effect on the methane yield. When the oxygen load-
ings during the hydrogen fermentation stage were 5, 10, 20, and
40 mL/g VS, the methane yields in the methane fermentation stage

were 287.8, 296.0, 285.5, and 270.6 mL/g VS (37 C and normal
pressure), which were 8.8%,11.9%, 7.9%, and 2.3% higher than that of
Two-stage 0, respectively. However, the positive effect really
depended on the oxygen loading level. In this study, the oxygen
loading of 10 mL/g VS during the hydrogen fermentation stage
resulted in the maximum methane yield in the methane fermen-
tation stage. After AD, the VS degradation rates of Two-stage 0,
Two-stage 5, Two-stage 10, Two-stage 20, Two-stage 40 and One-
stage were 65.3%, 73.3%, 74.2%, 71.2%, 69.2% and 60.2%, respec-
tively. The VS degradation rate data was quite corresponding to the
methane production results. Two-stage AD of corn straw obtained
higher VS degradation rate, and microaeration during hydrogen
fermentation could further improve the VS degradation rate.
Maximum VS degradation rate was obtained when the oxygen
loading during the hydrogen fermentation stage was 10 mL/g VS,
which was 23.2% and 13.7% higher than those of One-stage and
Two-stage without microaeration.
The positive effect of limited oxygen addition during the
hydrogen fermentation on the methane yield could attribute to two
reasons. Firstly, the microaerobic condition during the hydrogen
fermentation generated more available substrate than the anaer-
obic condition (e.g., VFAs shown in Fig. 3) for methanogenesis.
Secondly, the complex structure of the corn straw was destroyed
more during microaerobic hydrogen fermentation, making the corn
straw more available to biodegradation for methane production.
However, high oxygen loading during the hydrogen fermentation
stage did not necessarily lead to high methane yield, which could
be explained by the excessive oxidation of the substrates. Similar

results were obtained in both our previous studies (Fu et al., 2015,
2016b) and other research (Lim and Wang, 2013; Mshandete et al.,
2005). According to the methane yields data in this study, a two-
stage AD by combination of microaerobic hydrogen fermentation
and anaerobic methane fermentation could be a potential strategy
to produce bioenergy from corn straw, both the hydrogen and
methane production efﬁciencies could be improved signiﬁcantly. In
addition, there is no additional chemical (except limited oxygen or
air) needed during this procedure, which is more environmental
friendly.
3.3.2. Methane production characteristics
The methane production characteristics were described with
the parameters of P, Rm, l, and T80 (T80 is technical time, which
represents the time needed to produce 80% of the total methane
yield). The P, Rm and l were obtained by ﬁtting the methane pro-
duction data with the Modiﬁed Gompertz equation (Wang et al.,
2018; Zhang et al., 2014). As shown in Table 2, all of the AD
groups had a lag-phase. The span of the lag-phase of the two-stage
AD was much lower than that of the one-stage AD probably because
of more available substrates produced during the hydrogen
fermentation stage of the two-stage AD (Yang et al., 2011). In
addition, limited oxygen supply during hydrogen fermentation
reduced the length of lag-phase of the two-stage AD. The maximum
daily methane yields of the two-stage AD were also higher than
that of the one-stage AD. The Two-stage 10 achieved the highest

3.4. Energy recovery from the two-stage and one-stage AD of corn
straw
Generally, the AD process could be divide into three steps
namely hydrolysis, acidiﬁcation and methanogenesis, which in-
volves four kinds of microorganisms, namely fermentative bacteria,
hydrogen-producing
bacteria,
acetate-forming
bacteria
and
methane-forming archaea (Luo et al., 2013; Xue et al., 2015).
However, the optimal
growth conditions of
microorganisms
involved in the AD process were different (e.g. fermentative bac-
teria, hydrogen-producing bacteria, acetate-forming bacteria prefer
a slight acid condition; methane-forming archaea prefer neutral or
slight alkali condition). Therefore, not all the microorganisms in AD
are working at the optimum condition. Two-stage AD, in which the
AD process is separated into the hydrolysis/acidogensis (stage I)
and methanogenesis (stage II) that are optimized individually,
could ensure the different microorganisms working at their opti-
mum condition. In addition, the hydrogen fermentation stage of
two-stage AD could also be considered as biological pretreatment
method for organic solid waste, during the hydrogen fermentation
hydrogen energy recovery as well as substrate pretreatment could
be achieved simultaneously. Therefore, the two-stage AD performs
better than one-stage AD in biogas production, which leads to
higher energy recovery. Akobi et al. (2016) reported that the energy
yields from the two-stage AD of extruded poplar wood were 33%
(liquid streams obtained from poplar wood pretreated using the
twin screw extrusion) and 18% (solid streams obtained from poplar
wood pretreated using the twin screw extrusion) higher than those
of the one-stage AD, respectively. Also in our previous study, the
two-stage AD of vinasse resulted in 13% higher energy yield than
that of the one-stage AD (Fu et al., 2017). In this study, energy re-
covery from the two-stage and one-stage AD of corn straw was
calculated according to Eq. (2) and the resluts are shown in Table 3.
Hydrogen yields of the Two-stage 0, Two-stage 5, Two-stage 10,
Two-stage 20, and Two-stage 40 were 13.6, 22.7, 15.1, 7.1, and
2.8 mL/g VS (37 C and normal pressure), respectively. Methane
yields of the Two-stage 0, Two-stage 5, Two-stage 10, Two-stage 20,
Two-stage 40, and One-stage were 264.5, 287.8, 296.0, 285.5, 270.6,
and 255.3 mL/g VS (37 C and normal pressure), respectively. The
corresponding energy recoveries of the Two-stage 0, Two-stage 5,
Two-stage 10, Two-stage 20, Two-stage 40, and the one-stage were
9.47, 10.41, 10.60, 10.13, 9.55, and 8.98 kJ/g VS. It is evident that the
two-stage AD generated higher energy recovery, and the microa-
eration during the hydrogen fermentation further enhanced the
energy recovery from the two-stage AD. The maximum energy
recovery was obtained from the Two-stage 10, which was 12% and
18% higher than those of the Two-stage 0 and the one-stage,
respectively.
4. Conclusions
Two-stage AD of corn straw including stepwise hydrogen
fermentation and methane production improved the overall energy
recovery statistically signiﬁcantly compared to the one-stage AD. In
addition, microaeration during the hydrogen fermentation further
enhanced the hydrogen/methane yields and energy recovery. The
beneﬁcial effect of microaeration depended on the oxygen loading
level. The maximum energy recovery was achieved by the combi-
nation of microaerobic hydrogen fermentation with the oxygen
loading of 10 mL/g VS and methane fermentation, which was 18%
higher than that of the one-stage AD. In addition, the length of the
lag-phase and the total methane fermentation period were signif-
icantly reduced by using the two-stage AD and further reduced by
adding microaeration. Therefore, the developed two-stage AD with
stepwise microaerobic hydrogen fermentation and methano-
genesis is a promising approach to maximize the energy recovery
from AD of cellulose substrates. However, further researches also
